name: Tanning drops (Isle of Paradise style)
lead: Tanning drops are concentrated sunless tanning products designed to be mixed into a moisturiser, serum or other skincare so the user can choose how deep the colour goes. The format is associated with brands such as Isle of Paradise, whose self-tanning drops went viral on TikTok around 2020.[2]

People use them to look tanned without UV exposure: adding drops to a face or body moisturiser gives a gradual, adjustable colour that can make skin look healthier and more even, and, as one looksmax.org poster puts it, can make eye and hair colour stand out more.[3]

Sunless tanners usually contain dihydroxyacetone (DHA) at about 3 to 5 percent, which reacts with amino acids in the dead outer skin layer; the colour is temporary and does not involve melanin or UV.[1] No clinical studies on tanning drops were found.

chain: DHA reacts with dead surface skin
Healthier-looking, glowing skin tone without UV
angle.text: The drops give a temporary tan whose depth the user controls by how much goes into the moisturiser. Users apply them to the face or body for a bronzed, even look that fades over several days.

infobox: Isle of Paradise (founder Jules Von Hep)

paras: The product is added to a base moisturiser, so the amount used affects how deep the colour builds. Gradual tanning lotions in which colour builds with repeated use are a related format.[1] Isle of Paradise's founder, Jules Von Hep, is described as a celebrity spray tan artist.[2]
DHA's browning reaction occurs in the outermost dead skin layer through a Maillard-type reaction and is independent of UV.[1] Erythrulose acts similarly but develops more slowly.[1]

A sponsored 2020 article in Glossy described Isle of Paradise as a two-year-old brand that had ranked first among self-tanning brands at Sephora and sold over a quarter of a million self-tanning drops in six months, with TikTok users' glow-up videos credited for much of the attention. The article is brand-sponsored and its claims are not independently verified.[2]

A looksmax.org thread suggests mixing face tanning drops into moisturiser before bed to wake up with a glow, saying the colour makes blue eyes and blonde hair stand out more and advising barrier cream around the hairline and eyebrows to avoid orange staining. Replies ask which product the poster uses and whether a darker face than body looks unnatural.[3]

The US FDA has approved DHA for external use but not around the eyes, on lips or mucous membranes, or by inhalation.[1] Skin is reported to be more susceptible to UV for about 24 hours after DHA, and DHA can cause contact dermatitis; sunscreen in tanners may fade before the colour does.[1]

timeline.event: Sponsored coverage reports Isle of Paradise self-tanning drops topping Sephora's self-tanning category.[2]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, face tanning drops are mentioned as a simple way to add glow, with replies asking about brands and realism.[3]

claims.claim: Mixing tanning drops into night moisturiser makes the face look better by morning.
claims.believers: A poster says it makes eyes and hair stand out and gives a glow, while warning against overdoing it.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes DHA tanning as a temporary surface colour change; no studies were found on drops or on attractiveness effects.[1]

claims.claim: A darker face than body looks fake.
claims.believers: A reply on the thread asks whether a face darker than the rest of the body will look fake.[3]
claims.experts: No studies were found on this.

card.summary: Self-tan concentrate drops mixed into a moisturiser to build a custom colour, with no independent research on them.
card.note: DHA colour is temporary and fades in about 3 to 10 days.

quick.overview:
Tanning drops are concentrated self-tanning products added to a person's own lotion or skincare so that colour deepens with the amount used. Isle of Paradise is one brand associated with the format.

The format is not discussed in the encyclopedic sources reviewed, and no clinical studies were found.
quick.mechanism: Self-tanners generally rely on DHA, which reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin in a Maillard-type browning reaction, with no UV or melanin involved.[1]
quick.risks: DHA colour fades over roughly 3 to 10 days, and misapplication can produce orange or splotchy results.[1] Skin may be more UV-susceptible for about 24 hours after DHA use, and contact dermatitis is reported.[1]
